analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain to oil and gas drilling.
analysis.headline: A bill to open 1.5 million acres of the Arctic refuge's coastal plain to oil leasing was introduced in February 1989 and never received a committee or floor vote in the two years remaining in that Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended a 1920 leasing law to order the Interior Department to set up a competitive oil and gas leasing program on the 1.5 million acres of public land in the Coastal Plain of Alaska's North Slope — the part of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge that a 1980 law set aside for study. It would have required a first lease sale within twelve months, accepted a completed 1987 environmental review in place of any further studies, and cut off other land-management review. It also directed aid to Alaska communities affected by development and authorized talks with Canada about joint Arctic oil planning.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain access to leases on what the bill itself calls the nation's most promising onshore oil prospect, with estimated in-place reserves of 4.8 to 29.4 billion barrels, on tracts of up to 2,560 acres with ten-year initial terms. The bill directs the Secretary to "seek to maximize the revenue paid to the Treasury" while giving independent producers a competitive chance to bid. North Slope communities would receive federal impact aid for public services, Alaska would gain jobs and tax revenue, and consumers would benefit indirectly if new domestic supply lowered fuel prices — a claim the bill makes but that its own findings undercut, since it acknowledges a ten-or-more-year lead time before any new oil field produces.

how_it_helps.text: Would have created a competitive leasing program on 1.5 million acres of the Coastal Plain, with the first lease sale required within twelve months of enactment, opening the area to oil exploration, development, and production.
Would have directed the Interior Secretary to provide impact aid and planning help so North Slope communities could handle the public-service demands of oil development.

Cites national-security, consumer-price, and trade-balance benefits from new domestic production outside OPEC's influence, and projects new federal revenue from bonus bids, rents, and royalties deposited in the Treasury.

Requires that leasing and development achieve the "reasonable protection" of fish and wildlife, the environment, and subsistence users, and would have authorized US-Canada discussions on joint planning and transportation for Arctic oil and gas.

analysis.who_pays: The public owns the land being leased: 1.5 million acres of the Arctic refuge's coastal plain, the calving grounds of the Porcupine caribou herd and a habitat used by subsistence communities, would be opened to industrial development on a permanent basis. The bill would treat a 1987 study and environmental statement as satisfying all legal review requirements and state that \"no further studies, reports, or assessments shall be required\" and that no land-management review applies beyond the act itself, leaving the pace and terms of development largely to the Interior Secretary's discretion. Wildlife, the refuge ecosystem, and subsistence users would bear the environmental risk, while any consumer price benefit would arrive, at best, a decade later.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through the Arctic refuge itself

drawbacks.text: The bill would have permanently opened the wildest part of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to industrial development; the oil would be a public resource sold to private companies, and by the bill's own findings any new field would take ten or more years to develop, so it offered no near-term relief for consumers.

It would have short-circuited environmental review by declaring the 1987 Coastal Plain Resource Assessment and its environmental impact statement sufficient for all leasing decisions and stating that no further studies or land-management reviews were required — leaving protection of wildlife and subsistence uses dependent on discretionary conditions set by the Interior Secretary.

Supporters would also have to acknowledge genuine spill and habitat risk: the bill's answer is that eighteen years of Prudhoe Bay operations show development is "compatible" with wildlife, but the Coastal Plain is an undisturbed area that the 1980 Alaska lands act had deliberately set aside pending a study of exactly this question.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are real but concentrated: leasehold profits for oil companies, revenue and jobs for Alaska, and a modest addition to domestic supply years down the road. The cost is one-directional and permanent — the undeveloped heart of the nation's largest wildlife refuge, with its caribou, birds, and subsistence uses, would be committed to industrial development on the strength of a single completed review, with further study barred by the bill itself. Weighing those honestly, the bill traded an irreversible public-land decision for benefits that were speculative on the timeline the bill's own findings describe.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when that Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Frank Murkowski introduced the bill on February 28, 1989, with Senator Ted Stevens as cosponsor; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day.
The Energy and Natural Resources Committee never held a markup, reported the bill out, or scheduled it for a Senate vote; the action history shows no activity after the referral.
The bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, having received no vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Coastal Plain of the Arctic refuge stayed undeveloped, and the 1980 arrangement leaving its future to a federal study remained intact. Environmental and wilderness advocates got the outcome they wanted; the oil companies that backed opening the refuge got nothing from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Arctic refuge's coastal plain stayed undeveloped

for.name: Frank H. Murkowski
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to open the Coastal Plain to oil and gas leasing.

for.name: 2 of 45 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrats signed on.

for.name: Alaska's oil industry
for.what_they_did: Long pressed Congress to open the Arctic refuge's coastal plain to leasing, the policy this bill would have implemented.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee (Chair J. Bennett Johnston, D-LA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill; it sat in committee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Environmental and wilderness advocacy groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and worked to keep the Coastal Plain off the development path.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Republican senators cosponsored the bill and no Democrat did, but with no committee action or vote ever taken, the chamber as a whole never showed where it stood.

industries.note: The bill would have handed companies competitive leases on 1.5 million acres of federal land holding an estimated 4.8 to 29.4 billion barrels of oil in place, while barring further land-management review. The industry's gain came from converting protected public wilderness into private leaseholds; the bill died, so the industry gained nothing.

The bill leaned on the existing Trans-Alaska pipeline and tanker system to serve new Coastal Plain production and authorized joint US-Canada planning, including private tanker transport of Canadian Arctic crude along Alaska's coast. New production would have meant more volume and revenue for transport operators.

industries.industry: North Slope local governments and subsistence communities
industries.note: The bill promised federal impact aid to pay for public services strained by development and cited support from the North Slope Borough, Kaktovik, and Inupiat communities. Those same communities would have borne the effects of development on the wildlife and lands they rely on for subsistence.
